config.title: Accordion

intro.title: Accordion
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple accordion component that allows users to expand and collapse sections of content. You will learn how to manage component state in React to track which section is currently open. The main technologies and constructs involved are React's useState hook for state management and TypeScript for type safety. By the end, you'll have a functional accordion that toggles content visibility with a click.
intro.usecase: Accordions are essential UI patterns for managing content density in modern applications. You'll find them in FAQ sections, where they collapse answers under clickable questions, and in dashboard settings panels that hide advanced options until needed. They're also common in mobile navigation menus, product filter interfaces on e-commerce sites, and multi-step forms where sections expand as users progress. As a developer, implementing accordions helps you create cleaner, more organized interfaces that improve user experience by reducing cognitive load and screen clutter.

objectives: Construct a React component with TypeScript to manage accordion state
Initialize and update state to control which accordion item is expanded
Implement click handlers to toggle accordion sections
Render dynamic content based on the current accordion state
Apply conditional styling to visually indicate expanded and collapsed states
Bind keyboard interactions for accessibility in the accordion component
Configure the accordion to allow only one item expanded at a time (single-mode)

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the useState hook.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports are added at the top of the file.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the Accordion component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Accordion that returns null for now.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function with the name Accordion and have it return null.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the Accordion component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The Accordion component is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: A functional component named Accordion exists and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the Accordion component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a component named Accordion that returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've named it Accordion and it returns null.

steps.title: Define the accordion items data
steps.instruction: Inside your Accordion component, define a typed array of objects named **accordionItems** with title and content properties. Use an interface for type safety.
steps.hint: Create an interface for the item structure, then declare a constant array with at least two items containing title and content strings.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a properly typed `accordionItems` array ready to use for rendering accordion sections.
successCriteria: An interface for accordion items is defined, and a constant array named `accordionItems` with at least two objects containing title and content properties exists.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have both an interface and an array named `accordionItems` with title and content properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you defined an interface and created an `accordionItems` array with the correct structure.

steps.title: Initialize state for active item
steps.instruction: Inside your Accordion component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'activeIndex' that tracks which accordion item is expanded. Initialize it with null (meaning no item is active initially).
steps.hint: Call useState with null as the initial value and destructure the returned array into a state variable and setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: state for tracking selected item
const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<number | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a state variable 'activeIndex' that can hold either a number (for the index of the expanded item) or null (when all items are collapsed).
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with null as initial value, and the destructured state variable is named 'activeIndex'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with null and naming the state variable 'activeIndex'.
steps.feedbackWrong: call useState with null to create a state variable named 'activeIndex' inside the component.

steps.title: Create toggle handler function
steps.instruction: Inside the Accordion component, create a function named handleToggle that takes an index parameter of type number and toggles the active state by updating the activeIndex state.
steps.hint: Define a function that receives an index and uses setActiveIndex to update the state. You can check if the clicked index is already active to close it, or set it as active.
steps.expectedOutcome: A typed handler function that toggles the active accordion item index.
successCriteria: The handleToggle function is defined with a number parameter and updates activeIndex state appropriately.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but make sure it takes a number parameter and properly toggles the activeIndex state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggle handler function is missing or doesn't match the expected structure. Try creating a function named handleToggle that accepts an index parameter.

steps.title: Add container markup
steps.instruction: In your Accordion component, return a div element that will serve as the main container for the accordion.
steps.hint: Replace the current return statement with a div element. This div will wrap all the accordion items you'll add later.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a div container element instead of null.
successCriteria: The Accordion component returns a div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning a div element from the component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a div element to serve as the container for the accordion items.

steps.title: Define accordionItems
steps.instruction: Inside **Accordion**, **above** the `return`, declare **`const accordionItems`**: an array of **at least three** objects, each with **`title`** and **`content`** string properties (use the same shape as your item interface from the earlier step). Example titles: `'Section 1'`, `'Section 2'`, `'Section 3'`. If you already added **accordionItems** in step 3, extend it to **three or more** entries (or replace with three section objects) before mapping.
steps.hint: Pattern: `const accordionItems: YourInterface[] = [ { title: '...', content: '...' }, ... ];` Type the array with your interface name for safety.
steps.expectedOutcome: `accordionItems` exists with three or more objects, each with `title` and `content`, ready to map in JSX.
successCriteria: A constant named `accordionItems` holds an array of objects with `title` and `content`.
The array has at least three entries.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Data in place — next you'll render one row per entry with `.map`.
steps.feedbackPartial: Declare `const accordionItems` before the return, with at least three `{ title, content }` objects.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add something like: `const accordionItems = [ { title: 'Section 1', content: '...' }, { title: 'Section 2', content: '...' }, { title: 'Section 3', content: '...' } ];`

steps.title: Map through accordionItems
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, use the map method to iterate through the accordionItems array and render a div for each item. For now, just render a simple div with the item's title inside.
steps.hint: You can use the map method on the accordionItems array. Inside the map callback, return a JSX element (like a div) containing the item's title.
steps.expectedOutcome: The accordion container will display three div elements, each showing a section title (e.g., 'Section 1', 'Section 2', 'Section 3').
successCriteria: The map method is used on accordionItems
Each item renders a div with its title
A key prop is provided for each rendered element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using the map method on accordionItems and returning a div with the item's title for each element. Don't forget to add a key prop.
steps.feedbackWrong: use the map method on the accordionItems array inside the return statement. For each item, return a div containing the title property.

steps.title: Create accordion item structure
steps.instruction: Inside the map callback, return a div for each accordion item containing a button (for the title) and a content div.
steps.hint: The button should display the item's title, and the content div should display the item's content.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: mapping to create item structure items.map(item => (
{item.description}
))
steps.expectedOutcome: Each accordion item will have a button for its title and a div for its content, ready for styling and interactivity.
successCriteria: The map callback returns a div containing a button with the item's title and a div with the item's content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure each item has both a button (for title) and a div (for content).
steps.feedbackWrong: The structure is missing. Each mapped item should return a div containing a button and a content div.

steps.title: Add toggle button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Inside the map callback, add a button element with the item's title as its text content and wire its onClick to call the toggle handler with the current index.
steps.hint: The button should be the first element inside the div returned by the map callback. Use onClick={() => handleToggle(index)} to call the handler with the index.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: button with click handler
<button onClick={() => handleClick(itemId)}>
  Click me
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: Each accordion item will have a button displaying its title that triggers the toggle handler when clicked.
successCriteria: A button element is added inside the map callback with the item's title as its text content and an onClick handler that calls handleToggle with the index.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but make sure it has the correct text content and onClick handler that calls handleToggle with the index.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not properly configured. Add a button with the item's title and an onClick handler that calls handleToggle(index).

steps.title: Conditionally display content based on state
steps.instruction: Inside the map function, add conditional rendering to show the content div only when the current item index matches the activeIndex state.
steps.hint: Use a ternary operator to conditionally render the content div. The condition should check if activeIndex equals the current index.
steps.expectedOutcome: The accordion content will only be visible for the active item when clicked, and hidden when another item is clicked or when closed.
successCriteria: Content div is conditionally rendered using a ternary operator
Condition checks if activeIndex equals current index
Content displays only when condition is true
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your conditional logic. Make sure you're comparing activeIndex with the current index and using a ternary operator to conditionally render the content div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional rendering isn't working correctly. Review how to use ternary operators in JSX and ensure you're comparing the activeIndex state with the current item index.
